title: Why Are Claim Charts Required and Basics of How They Are Prepared (IIPRD)

extracted.subtask_short: Evidence-type hierarchy for claim-to-reference mapping strength
extracted.subtask_description: Defines a taxonomy of evidence types (direct references, indirect/backend-logic inference, standard mapping, source code, teardowns, reverse engineering, doctrine of equivalents) used to fill the mapping column of a claim chart, and an implied confidence hierarchy for how strongly each type supports a claim-element match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct references — dated, authenticated product documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather official product documents, datasheets, marketing materials, videos, and related publications from the target company/publisher, verifying source authenticity and publication dates. For invalidity purposes, date verification is not optional — it is what makes the reference qualify as prior art at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as the second-strongest evidence type in the informal hierarchy, just below source code/teardown/reverse-engineering evidence, provided the documentation is dated and authenticated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect references — backend-logic inference mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct claim-element disclosure isn't found, evaluate whether backend logic implies use of the claimed feature. For instance, if a product advertises secure transactions without explicitly mentioning a specific encryption algorithm, backend analysis might reveal the claimed method is necessarily used to achieve the advertised functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flagged as a weaker, inference-based mapping that typically needs corroborating technical analysis (source code, teardown) rather than resting on the inference alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard mapping (SEP claim charts) — essentiality and compliance as separate steps
rubrics_metrics.description: For Standard Essential Patents, employ a two-step test: (1) locate documents revealing technical-standard usage/requirements, then (2) map patent claims to demonstrate the patent's essentiality to that standard, and separately show the accused product also complies with the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essentiality mapping (claim-to-standard) and compliance mapping (standard-to-product) are treated as two distinct steps, each independently supportable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source code review — highest-confidence evidence for software claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented inventions claiming algorithms or underlying logic, examine source code to uncover embedded algorithms — tracing "data flow and operations, understanding the decision-making process, and ascertaining how different components interact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is treated as the highest-confidence evidence type for software claims, since it shows the actual implementation rather than a marketing description of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teardown reports for mechanical/apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For mechanical or apparatus claims, disassemble products to reveal underlying components and connections, enabling comprehensive comparison with patent claims (e.g., analyzing a foldable smartphone's hinge mechanism against a claimed hinge structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering for semiconductor claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For semiconductor inventions, reverse engineering deconstructs chips to analyze layered structures, logic gates, and data paths, determining whether the device's structure matches claimed specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents as fallback disclosure channel
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim elements aren't literally disclosed, infringement may still exist under the doctrine of equivalents if "the accused product or process contain[s] elements identical or equivalent to each claimed element" — requiring analysis of whether the substitute element matches the claimed element's function, way, and result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as the fallback rung of the evidence hierarchy, invoked only when literal/explicit disclosure of a specific element is unavailable, and requiring its own function/way/result showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal evidence-strength hierarchy for mapping confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: This source implies an informal evidence hierarchy for how confidently a mapping can be asserted: (1) Strongest — source code/teardown/reverse-engineering evidence directly showing the claimed structure or algorithm; (2) Strong — direct, dated, authenticated product documentation or publication explicitly describing the feature; (3) Weaker — indirect/backend-logic inference or standard-compliance inference, requiring an explicit secondary showing rather than being asserted on their own; (4) Fallback — Doctrine of Equivalents, invoked only when literal/explicit disclosure is unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chart entry that relies on evidence lower in this hierarchy without the accompanying corroboration is the practical signature of a "stretch" mapping rather than a genuine match.
